<section begin=par51/>''{{hyphenated word end|self|oneself}}'', e.g. {{GHGheb|text=נִשְׁאַל|translate=to ask}} (something) ''for oneself'' ({{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=20|verse=6.28}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Neh|chapter=13|verse=6}}), cf. {{polytonic|αἰτοῦμαί σε τοῦτο}}, {{polytonic|ἐνδύσασθαι χιτῶνα}} ''to put on'' (oneself) ''a tunic''.

{{GHGmargin-letter|51|f}}
(''d'') In consequence of a looseness of thought at an early period of the language, {{GHGterm|Niphʿal}} comes finally in many cases to represent the {{GHGterm|passive}}<ref>Cf. Halfmann, {{GHGcite|title=Beiträge zur Syntax der hebräischen Sprache}}, I. Stück, Wittenb., 1888, 2. St. 1892 (Gymn.-Programm), statistics of the Niphʿal (Puʿal, Hophʿal, and qāṭûl) forms at different periods of the language, for the purpose of ascertaining the meaning of Niph. and its relation to the passive; the selection of periods is, however, very questionable from the standpoint of literary criticism.</ref> of {{GHGterm|Qal}}, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=יָלַד|translate=to bear}}, Niph. ''to be born''; {{GHGheb|text=קָבַר|translate=to bury}}, Niph. ''to be buried''. In cases where {{GHGterm|Qal}} is intransitive in meaning, or is not used, {{GHGterm|Niphʿal}} appears also as the passive of {{GHGterm|Piʿēl}} and {{GHGterm|Hiphʿîl}}, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=כָּבֵד|translate=to be in honour}}, Piʿēl ''to honour'', Niph. ''to be honoured'' (as well as Puʿal {{GHGheb|text=כֻּבַּד}}); {{GHGheb|text=כָּחַד}} Piʿēl ''to conceal'', Hiph. ''to destroy'', Niph. passive of either. In such cases {{GHGterm|Niphʿal}} may again coincide in meaning with Qal ({{GHGheb|text=חָלָה}} Qal and Niph. ''to be ill'') and even take an accusative.

{{GHGmargin-letter|51|g}}
Examples of denominatives are, {{GHGheb|text=נִזְכַּר|translate=to be born a male}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=34|verse=19}} (from {{GHGheb|text=זָכָר}}; but probably {{GHGheb|text=הַזָּכָר}} should here be read); {{GHGheb|text=נִלְבַּב|translate=cordatum fieri|en=to become hearty}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=11|verse=12}} (from {{GHGheb|text=לֵבָב|translate=cor|en=heart}}); doubtless also {{GHGheb|text=נִבְנָה|translate=to obtain children}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=16|verse=2}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=30|verse=3|hidebook=1}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|51|h}}
The older grammarians were decidedly wrong in representing {{GHGterm|Niphʿal}} simply as the {{GHGterm|passive}} of {{GHGterm|Qal}}; for {{GHGterm|Niphʿal}} has (as the frequent use of its imperat. shows), in no respect the character of the other passives, and in Arabic a special conjugation (''ʾinqătălă'') corresponds to it with a passive of its own. Moreover, the forms mentioned in {{GHGpar|52|e}} point to a differently formed passive of {{GHGterm|Qal}}.—The form {{GHGheb|text=נְגֹֽאֲלוּ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=59|verse=3}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=La|chapter=4|verse=14}}, is not to be regarded as a passive of Niphʿal, but with König and Cheyne as a ''forma mixta'', in the sense that the punctuators intended to combine two optional readings, {{GHGheb|text=נִגְאֲלוּ}}, perf. Niph., and {{GHGheb|text=גֹּֽאֲלוּ}}, perf. Puʿal [cf. also Wright, {{GHGcite|title=Compar. Gramm.}}, p. 224]. Although the passive use of Niphʿal was introduced at an early period, and became tolerably common, it is nevertheless quite secondary to the reflexive use.

{{GHGmargin-letter|51|i}}
Rem. 1. The ''infin. absol.'' {{GHGheb|text=נִקְטוֹל}} is connected in form with the perfect, to which it bears the same relation as {{GHGheb|text=קָטוֹל}} to {{GHGheb|text=קָטַל}} in Qal, the ''ô'' in the second syllable being obscured from an original ''â''. Examples are, {{GHGheb|text=נִכְסֹף}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=31|verse=30}}; {{GHGheb|text=נִלְחֹם}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=11|verse=25}}; {{GHGheb|text=נִשְׁאֹל}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=20|verse=6.28}}, all in connexion with the perfect.

{{GHGmargin-letter|51|k}}
Examples of the form {{GHGheb|text=הִקָּטֹל}} (in connexion with imperfects) are, {{GHGheb|text=הִנָּתֹן}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=32|verse=4}}; {{GHGheb|text=הֵֽאָכֹל}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=7|verse=18}}; once {{GHGheb|text=אִדָּרֹשׁ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=14|verse=3}}, where, perhaps, the subsequent {{GHGheb|text=אִדָּרֵשׁ}} has led to the substitution of {{GHGheb|text=א}} for {{GHGheb|text=ה}}.—Moreover, the form {{GHGheb|text=הִקָּטֵל}} is not infrequently used also for the infin. absol.,<ref>But, like {{GHGheb|text=הִקָּטֹל}}, ''only'' in connexion with imperfects, except {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=7|verse=9}}. Barth is therefore right in describing ({{GHGcite|title=Nominalbildung}}, p. 74) both forms as later analogous formations (in addition to the original Semitic {{GHGheb|text=נִקְטוֹל}}), intended to assimilate the infinitive to the imperfect which it strengthens.</ref> e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=22|verse=3}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=15|verse=31}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=4|verse=26}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=20|verse=39}}. On the other hand, {{GHGheb|text=כְּהִנָּדֵף}} should simply be read for the wholly abnormal {{GHGheb|text=כְּהִנְדֹּף}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=68|verse=3}} (commonly explained as being intended to correspond in sound with the subsequent {{GHGheb|text=תִּנְדֹּף}}, but probably a ‘forma mixta’, combining the readings {{GHGheb|text=כְּהִנָּדֵף}} and {{GHGheb|text=כִּנְדֹף}}).
